items.title: [npr.org] Alaska Native villages remain displaced a year after Typhoon Halong
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

A year after the remnants of Typhoon Halong destroyed homes and infrastructure in western Alaska, residents of Kipnuk and Kwigillingok remain displaced as repairs continue, with many unsure when they can return. The October 2025 storm affected more than 40 communities, and about 1,500 people were evacuated from Kwigillingok, Kipnuk and Nightmute. Alaska officials estimate that federal aid will make most Kipnuk homes livable by Thanksgiving, but say some residents need replacement housing. The state is seeking more funding. Both Kipnuk and Kwigillingok voted to relocate to higher ground, but current disaster funding is not designed to pay for moving the communities.

Kipnuk homes: Alaska’s Emergency Operations Center estimated 90% of Kipnuk residences were damaged; the town has fewer than 200 homes and is consistently accessible mainly by plane (npr.org).

items.title: [cbc.ca] Canadian police suspend use of Crime Stoppers after 1.5 million records exposed
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Canadian police services are suspending their use of Crime Stoppers after a breach exposed more than 1.5 million tips submitted across Canada over 25 years, a CBC News investigation found. More than 850,000 records included personally identifiable information. The tips were managed through P3, software provided by U.S.-based Navigate360. Navigate360 acknowledged on Friday that its database had been breached between November 2025 and March 2026 and said potentially exposed information included names, addresses, birth dates and Social Security numbers. The company said it had no evidence the information had been used for fraud or identity theft. Police in several provinces have paused their use of the service while they assess the breach and its safeguards. Toronto and Ottawa police are directing people to report information through police channels, which do not necessarily offer the same anonymity. Crime Stoppers chapters and police are seeking further details from Navigate360. The company said it hired a cybersecurity firm to help strengthen security.

items.title: [theguardian.com] Ceasefire lets hundreds flee occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Hundreds of civilians evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky reached Ukrainian-held territory on Saturday, Oct. 31, after a local ceasefire allowed them to leave and aid to enter. U.S. First Lady Melania Trump mediated the pause, while Pope Leo XIV urged access for aid and evacuations. The ceasefire began Tuesday in the southern Kherson region and was scheduled to end Sunday evening. Residents travelled by bus through occupied Crimea to Russia, then flew to Belarus and crossed into Ukraine’s Chernihiv region, where relatives and aid workers met them. Some evacuees said food supplies had run out and they had survived on garden plants. The ceasefire also allowed roads to be cleared of mines and food and medicine to enter Oleshky. items.title: [Fast Company] Hackers hijacked a Claude Code extension, exposing yet another new AI security risk
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The world can feel particularly unsafe these days, with AI agents running rampant within private networks and billions of dollars disappearing from crypto wallets in less time than it takes to watch a sitcom episode.

But while the world was watching Binance’s massive crypto heist, another potentially consequential security breach was unfolding largely under the radar.

For roughly 11 hours, a malicious version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension was available on Cursor’s VS Code extension marketplace. The extension—which allows developers to use Anthropic’s AI coding assistant within Cursor to write, edit, and debug software—had been tampered with to collect information about users’ computers and attempt to install a persistent backdoor. That backdoor used Secure Shell (SSH), a tool for remotely accessing computers, and could potentially have allowed hackers to access victims’ machines even after the extension was removed.

Cursor disclosed the breach in a blog post, saying it removed the compromised extension as soon as it discovered the problem. The company also emphasized that the mechanism intended to give hackers remote access was unlikely to have worked in many cases because of flaws in its code. Anthropic, meanwhile, said in a statement that the incident “only impacts Cursor users” and was unrelated to Anthropic’s own systems.

According to Cursor’s security notice, the malicious extension was designed to leave behind scripts that would attempt to reconnect to the hackers’ server every minute, even after the extension had been removed. Cursor says it has since worked with the server’s hosting provider to take the server offline and to temporarily shut down and rebuild its extension marketplace. The company found no evidence that other extensions were compromised. Still, it is urging anyone who installed the affected version on October 29 to check their computers for signs of infection, remove any unauthorized access, and consider changing potentially compromised credentials.

The hackers’ identities remain unknown, but security experts say the incident illustrates an increasingly troubling risk as AI coding tools become embedded in developers’ workflows.

“The scenario of Claude sending out poisoned agents everywhere makes me even more worried than I already was,” says Eerke Boiten, a professor of cybersecurity at De Montfort University in England.

Gwen van der Velden, a professor of education at the University of Warwick who’s working on a program to help rebuild Ukraine, says the choice of the Claude Code extension is particularly “interesting” given the potential for such tools to be exploited in hybrid warfare.

“We know from the Russian side, it is of great interest to them,” she says. “If you were to go for hybrid warfare, where you use this kind of technology, then actually getting 5,000 bits of malware reproducing itself through AI agents is a powerful thing.”

The broader concern isn’t simply that a malicious extension could compromise individual computers. It’s that the growing ecosystem of AI coding assistants and their associated tools is creating new pathways into sensitive systems.

“This is a classic example of how everyone has been focussing on LLMs attacking other systems, yet forgetting about the fact that LLMs and their associated tools are increasing the attack surface across some very sensitive IT estates,” says Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at the University of Surrey.

And even a relatively limited breach could carry outsized consequences when the targets are software developers with access to sensitive code and infrastructure.

“While 5,000 users might sound relatively small, these are developers who have access to highly sensitive systems and source code, so the potential impact will be far greater than the numbers suggest,” says Jake Moore, a threat adviser with the global cybersecurity firm ESET. “Software extensions have eased their way into many people’s workflows, but the concern is how easily trusted software extensions can become a vehicle for malicious code.”

items.title: [cw39.com] Researchers favor permanent standard time as US debates clock changes
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Most U.S. clocks turn back one hour Nov. 1, as new research reviews renew debate over whether year-round standard time or daylight saving time better supports health. A Canadian policy analysis and a review focused on people with mental illness argue that permanent standard time better protects sleep, mood and biological rhythms. A broader review of population studies, however, finds a mix of harms and benefits from seasonal clock changes and summer daylight saving time. Permanent daylight saving time would delay winter sunrise, while permanent standard time would bring earlier summer sunrises and winter sunsets. The U.S. House passed a bill to make daylight saving time permanent in July 2026, but the Senate has not taken it up. The next seasonal clock change is scheduled for March 14, 2027.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government sent 500 additional soldiers to Milan and approved tougher measures involving minors. On Saturday, police also detained 30-year-old freelance journalist Youssef Siher, suspected of organizing the 17 October Movement. They searched more than 150 locations in Milan, Monza and about 20 other cities as part of investigations into the earlier unrest.

items.title: [farmer.pl] Farmers urged to shred corn stalks to curb pests and disease
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

As Poland’s corn harvest continues, agronomic guidance recommends finely shredding stalks and other crop residues after harvest to reduce winter shelter for the European corn borer and limit disease in the next season. The borer’s larvae overwinter in stalks, while feeding damage can promote Fusarium infections that contaminate grain with mycotoxins. Residue management also affects soil organic matter: grain corn leaves substantial biomass in the field, while silage harvesting removes nearly all above-ground material. Guidance recommends accounting for soil moisture and the next crop; working wet soil can cause compaction, and fields vulnerable to erosion may need residue left on the surface.

items.title: [LoRaMeshDevices] This Tiny Meshtastic Node Is Solar Ready: Base Uno First Look
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The Muzi Works Base Uno caught my attention because it packs quite a few useful features into a very small Meshtastic board. It comes pre-flashed, includes a 1,500 mAh battery, and has dedicated connections for a solar panel. That is a pretty interesting starting point for a little off-grid node. I bought the kit to find out how easily it would get going and whether the solar input actually worked. By the end of my first round of testing, it had connected over Bluetooth, discovered nearby nodes, completed a traceroute, and charged its battery to around 96% using a small solar panel. So far, this little board is looking good. Key Takeaways The Base Uno kit includes a pre-flashed Meshtastic board, antenna, and 1,500 mAh three-wire LiPo battery. Bluetooth pairing worked with PIN 123456, and I retained Long Fast to match my existing mesh. A small solar panel connected to PV+ and ground raised the reported battery level to about 96%. The app eventually showed 33 online nodes, and a traceroute to a node roughly a mile away succeeded. Table of Contents What Comes in the Base Uno Kit? The Three-Wire Battery Is an Interesting Detail Hardware Connections for Expansion and Solar First Power-Up and Bluetooth Pairing Configuring LoRa to Match the Local Mesh Node Discovery Took a Little Patience Connecting a Small Solar Panel More Nodes and a Successful Traceroute A Mobile Node or a Permanent Solar Node? What Comes in the Base Uno Kit? The kit includes the essentials for getting the board powered up and connected: The Base Uno board, carrying Elecrow and Muzi Works branding. A small screw-on antenna. A USB cable. A 1,500 mAh rechargeable LiPo battery. A small Allen key and screws. The board itself is quite compact. There is a reset button and a user button, but no display. Configuration and status checks happen through the Meshtastic app rather than on a screen attached to the node. Its nRF processor is one reason I was interested in it. This is the sort of hardware I would expect to be light on battery use, which makes it appealing for both a portable device and a solar-powered installation. I have not measured its power consumption or battery runtime yet, though, so those remain things to test rather than results from this first look. The Three-Wire Battery Is an Interesting Detail The included battery stood out more than I expected. It is a 1,500 mAh LiPo with three wires, rather than just the usual positive and negative leads. The third wire is a sensing connection. My understanding is that it provides battery temperature information that the charging circuitry can use to manage charging, including stopping it when conditions are unsuitable. That is particularly interesting on a board intended for solar use. I like seeing that extra sensing connection, but I did not test the temperature cutoff or establish its operating thresholds. The important distinction here is that the battery offers more than a simple two-wire power connection. Confirming exactly how the board responds to that sensing input will need further testing. Hardware Connections for Expansion and Solar There is quite a bit available around the edges of this little board: QWIIC port: An expansion connection I plan to try in a separate test. SDA and SCL pins: The labeled I2C connections. TX and RX pins: Serial connections for additional projects. OLED-related connections: Useful options if a display becomes part of the build. PV+ and ground: The dedicated solar-panel connections. Battery connector: Located on the back of the board, separate from the QWIIC port. That last distinction is worth paying attention to during assembly. The battery does not plug into the QWIIC port. I checked the connector location and orientation before seating it in the battery socket on the back. The PV+ and ground connections are what make this especially tempting as a solar-node project. Rather than starting with a separate charging arrangement, there is already a place on the board to bring in the panel. First Power-Up and Bluetooth Pairing Connect the antenna before powering up the node. I screwed on the supplied antenna first, then connected the battery. An LED came on straight away, which was a good start. The package identified the board as pre-flashed with Meshtastic, so there was no initial firmware installation to work through. My setup sequence was straightforward: Attach the antenna. Plug the battery into the correct battery connector. Open the Meshtastic app and look for the node over Bluetooth. Select the discovered Meshtastic device. Enter the Bluetooth pairing PIN. Allow the app to load the node information. Because there is no display, I tried the default PIN, 123456, and it connected successfully. The Bluetooth settings later confirmed that this was the configured PIN. It can be changed there rather than left at the default. My unit arrived running Meshtastic 2.7.15. The app initially reported the battery at 45%, while a later device-metrics reading showed 67%. Those were the reported values during setup, not a controlled battery-capacity measurement. Changing the Node Name I went into the user settings and gave the node a recognizable name using my vervesoft.live naming scheme with a Muzi identifier. Saving the change caused the node to reboot. The Bluetooth connection dropped while it restarted, and the status LED changed colors before the node returned. The same behavior occurred when saving the LoRa settings. A brief disconnect after saving was part of the restart, not a failed setup. Configuring LoRa to Match the Local Mesh The board initially had the Long Fast modem preset selected. My other nodes were still using Long Fast, so I kept this board on the same settings for the first test. Selecting the US region in the app changed the preset to Long Turbo during this setup. I changed it back to Long Fast so the Base Uno would match my existing nodes. These were the US-region combinations shown during the test: Long Fast: Frequency slot 20, operating at 906.875 MHz. Long Turbo: Frequency slot 14, operating at 908.75 MHz. Long Turbo was the newer default I encountered at the time, but compatibility with the mesh I already had running was the immediate priority. There was no point leaving this one node on a different preset while the rest were still waiting to be migrated. Choose the correct region for your location and check that the radio settings match the nodes you intend to use. The US settings above describe this particular setup, not a configuration to copy regardless of country. Other Settings I Checked With the radio configured, I worked through the remaining settings: Channels: A Long Fast channel was already present. Position sharing: The installed firmware allowed it on that channel, with an approximately 1.8-mile position-precision radius shown. Device role: The board was set to Client. Time zone: I used the computer’s time zone. Buzzer: The configuration listed pin 22, although I did not add or test a buzzer. Display: Display settings were turned off. Bluetooth: The fixed PIN was set to 123456. There was no GPS installed on this setup, so the position-sharing option did not mean the board was producing its own GPS location. It also had no environmental readings available. Node Discovery Took a Little Patience At first, the node list stayed empty apart from the Base Uno itself. I enabled the option to include unknown nodes, but there was still nothing else immediately. I expected it to find somebody fairly quickly. Instead of changing everything at once, I left it running and checked a few diagnostics. The signal-quality page did not provide a noise-floor reading with the installed firmware. It did show transmit and receive counters, including one TX and one RX at that stage. Battery telemetry was available, but there was no environmental or position data. Then another node appeared, identified as 49D4. That was the first useful confirmation that the Base Uno was receiving another mesh node. More entries followed as it continued running. The practical lesson from this first startup was simple: an empty node list in the first few minutes did not turn out to mean the board was faulty. In this case, it needed a little time. I also checked the firmware version against the releases available at the time. The unit had 2.7.15, while 2.7.26 was listed as the latest stable release then. I left the firmware alone for this test so I could establish how the kit behaved as supplied. Connecting a Small Solar Panel Once the basic setup was working, I tried the feature that interested me most: solar charging. I took a small panel described as roughly 200 mA and soldered its leads to the PV+ and ground connections on the back of the board. The LiPo battery remained connected, and I placed the assembly outside for a short test. The first solar test used a small panel connected directly to the board’s dedicated solar input. This was a bare-board experiment, not a finished outdoor installation. I still need to find a suitable case before turning it into a permanent node. Solar Charging Results There was a useful amount of sun, followed by some cloud, so the panel did not have uninterrupted sunshine throughout the test. Even so, the reported battery level rose from readings in the 60% to 70% range earlier in the session to approximately 95% to 96%. The device-metrics graph showed the upward charging trend after the assembly had been outside. That is the encouraging result: the solar input worked, and the reported battery charge increased while the node was operating. This was not a measured charging-efficiency test, and it does not yet establish whether this particular panel can sustain the node through nights and poor weather. It does show that the basic solar-charging arrangement is functional. More Nodes and a Successful Traceroute After the board had been running outside for a while, the app showed 33 online nodes with unknown entries filtered out. That was quite a change from the nearly empty list during the first few minutes. I then requested a traceroute to another node, and it returned successfully. The other node was roughly a mile down the road, which was a pleasing result with the little supplied stubby antenna still attached. I would not turn that into a maximum-range claim. This was an initial connectivity check, not a controlled range test. Still, the board was doing the things I wanted to establish first: receiving mesh traffic and completing a traceroute. A Mobile Node or a Permanent Solar Node? That is now the interesting decision. The Base Uno is small enough to make a neat portable build, but the dedicated solar input makes a permanent solar node very tempting. For a mobile build, the compact board and included 1,500 mAh battery are appealing. For a solar build, the working panel input and three-wire battery sensing are the details that stand out. My next steps are to find a case, update the firmware, and test the QWIIC port. I also want more time with the power system before making any claims about long-term autonomy. For now, this is a very positive first impression. It booted, paired, accepted configuration changes, discovered nearby nodes, and charged from a small solar panel. That is a pretty good start for a tiny Meshtastic board. Affiliate disclosure: I may earn from qualifying purchases through the product link below.
